clinicalPearls: Symptoms vary by tumor location. Right-sided cancers (cecum, ascending colon) can grow large without obstruction because stool is still liquid, and they tend to ulcerate, causing chronic insidious blood loss and presenting as iron-deficiency anemia (Harrison 22e p.656).

Unexplained iron-deficiency anemia in any adult mandates a thorough endoscopic and/or radiographic visualization of the entire large bowel; the possible exception is a premenopausal, multiparous woman (Harrison 22e p.656).

Left-sided (transverse/descending colon) tumors impede passage of more formed stool, producing abdominal cramping, occasional obstruction, and even perforation, classically the annular constricting 'apple-core' lesion on imaging (Harrison 22e p.656).

Rectosigmoid cancers cause hematochezia, tenesmus, and narrowing of stool caliber; these may be mistaken for hemorrhoids, but rectal bleeding and/or altered bowel habits demand prompt digital rectal exam and sigmoidoscopy (Harrison 22e p.656).

Most colorectal cancers arise from adenomatous polyps (not hyperplastic, hamartomatous, or serrated polyps); only a minority of adenomas progress, with risk tied to polyp size and histology, and villous adenomas becoming cancer about threefold more often than tubular adenomas (Harrison 22e p.653).

Universal testing of colorectal tumors for MMR defects is recommended, by immunohistochemistry for MMR proteins or microsatellite instability testing; MSI-high tumors are dramatically sensitive to immune checkpoint inhibition and less sensitive to chemotherapy (Harrison 22e p.653-654, 656).

Serum CEA is used for staging workup and follow-up; some authorities measure plasma CEA at 3-month intervals after curative resection because of its sensitivity as a marker for otherwise undetectable recurrence (Harrison 22e p.656-658).

Liver is the most frequent visceral metastatic site, being the initial site of distant spread in about one-third of recurring cancers and involved in over two-thirds of patients at death; complete resection of metastases isolated to one site (liver, lung, peritoneum) is considered curative (Harrison 22e p.657-658).
harrison.pathophysiology: The majority of colorectal cancers develop through the adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence, in which adenomatous polyps accumulate sequential genetic and epigenetic events involving tumor suppressor genes and oncogenes. Three major sporadic molecular pathways exist: the chromosomal instability (CIN) pathway (the most common), characterized by early loss of the APC tumor suppressor gene followed by sequential MAP-kinase oncogene mutations such as KRAS and BRAF, with loss of p53 as a common final step; the mismatch repair (MMR) pathway, often caused by hypermethylation of MMR gene promoters, producing a microsatellite-instability-high (MSI-high) phenotype; and the CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP), with tumors that are often right-sided and associated with MLH1 methylation. These pathways are not mutually exclusive and can overlap in individual cancers (Harrison 22e p.653-654).
additionalDifferentials: Hemorrhoids or benign anorectal disease as a cause of rectal bleeding (rectal bleeding and altered bowel habits still demand DRE and sigmoidoscopy) (Harrison 22e p.656)
Other causes of iron-deficiency anemia from chronic occult GI blood loss (Harrison 22e p.656)
Inflammatory bowel disease (both a risk factor and a differential for altered bowel habit and bleeding) (Harrison 22e p.655)
additionalInvestigations: Colonoscopy of the entire large bowel (gold standard for detecting cancer and synchronous neoplasms/polyps) (Harrison 22e p.656)
Flexible sigmoidoscopy as a screening modality (Harrison 22e p.655-656)
Stool-based tests: fecal occult blood test, fecal immunochemical test (FIT), and fecal DNA testing (Harrison 22e p.655-656)
Complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel (Harrison 22e p.656)
Chest, abdomen, and pelvic CT scan; MRI and PET as dictated by CT findings (Harrison 22e p.656)
Pelvic MRI for rectal cancer to assess mesorectal margin and nodal status (Harrison 22e p.658)
Tumor MMR/microsatellite instability testing (IHC or MSI) and germline genetic testing where indicated (Harrison 22e p.654, 656)
Investigational: plasma circulating tumor DNA as a biomarker for residual/recurrent disease (Harrison 22e p.658)
redFlags: Unexplained iron-deficiency anemia in any adult (mandates evaluation of the entire large bowel)
Change in bowel habit / altered bowel habits
Tenesmus and narrowing of the caliber of the stool (rectosigmoid lesions)
Strong family history or known hereditary syndrome (FAP, MUTYH-associated polyposis, Lynch syndrome)
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis is stage-related and depends on depth of tumor penetration into the bowel wall, regional lymph node involvement, and distant metastases (TNM). Stage I (T1-2N0M0) confers a high cure rate (>90-95% 5-year survival); 5-year survival declines through stage II (T3-4N0M0), stage III (node-positive), and stage IV (distant metastasis, <5% in colon). Stage I patients are considered cured after complete resection. A minimum of 12 sampled lymph nodes is considered necessary to accurately define stage. Poor-prognosis features include penetration through the bowel wall into pericolic fat, poorly differentiated histology, perforation and/or adherence to adjacent organs, venous invasion, preoperative CEA >5 ng/mL, BRAF mutation, and right-sided primary location. Tumors with MSI/MMR defects have an improved prognosis (enhanced immune response), and left-colon tumors fare better than right-colon tumors. Notably, primary tumor size does not influence prognosis once adjusted for nodal involvement and differentiation. Most recurrences occur within the first 5 years (Harrison 22e p.656-658).
pitfalls: Attributing rectal bleeding to hemorrhoids and not pursuing DRE and sigmoidoscopy (Harrison 22e p.656)

Relying on fecal occult blood testing alone: about 50% of patients with documented colorectal cancer have a negative FOBT due to intermittent bleeding, and a colorectal neoplasm is NOT found in most asymptomatic individuals with a positive test (Harrison 22e p.655-656)
Sigmoidoscopy alone misses proximal lesions: about 1.5% of individuals with a normal sigmoidoscopy harbor a high-risk polyp or adenocarcinoma in the proximal colon (Harrison 22e p.656)
Lynch syndrome may not be associated with multiple polyps and is therefore often unrecognized (Harrison 22e p.654)
Disease stage cannot be determined accurately before surgical resection and pathologic analysis unless gross metastatic disease is present (Harrison 22e p.656)

Initial treatment should be delayed until MMR/microsatellite status is known when possible, since MSI-high rectal cancers may be cured with checkpoint inhibitors (PD-1 antibodies) without surgery, radiation, or chemotherapy (Harrison 22e p.656)
harrison.severityClassification: TNM classification (American Joint Committee on Cancer / Union for International Cancer Control): T = depth of tumor penetration (T1 submucosa, T2 muscularis, T3 through muscularis, T4 adjacent structures), N = regional lymph node involvement (N1 = 1-3 nodes, N2 = >=4 nodes), M = distant metastasis. Stage I = T1-2N0M0; Stage II = T3-4N0M0; Stage III = any T, N1-2, M0; Stage IV = any T, any N, M1. The older Dukes classification was historically used for colorectal cancer (Harrison 22e p.656).
management: Surgical resection with regional lymphadenectomy as the curative mainstay for localised colon and rectal cancer
Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for locally advanced rectal cancer to downstage before surgery
Adjuvant oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy such as FOLFOX or CAPOX for node-positive and high-risk node-negative disease
Systemic therapy for metastatic disease combining cytotoxic chemotherapy with targeted agents - anti-EGFR antibodies in RAS wild-type tumours and the anti-VEGF antibody bevacizumab
Immune checkpoint inhibition for mismatch-repair-deficient, microsatellite-instability-high tumours, guided by universal MMR and MSI testing
Post-treatment surveillance with serial carcinoembryonic antigen, colonoscopy and cross-sectional imaging
Management through a colorectal multidisciplinary team, with genetic counselling and family screening where a hereditary syndrome such as Lynch is identified
